original_question: For the Engel distribution, namely a rank-2 distribution on R^4 with n_3(q) = 3 and n_4(q) = 4, sub-Riemannian spheres are 3-dimensional hypersurfaces and every point lies on a unique singular curve whose small segments are optimal. What is the corresponding local classification of sphere singularities at points where such optimal singular curves meet the sphere?
target_in_paper: Section IV, Unfolding the sub-Riemannian distance: the unnumbered open question asking for a C^1-classification of germs of sub-Riemannian spheres at points reached by optimal singular curves, specialized immediately afterward to the Engel distribution in R^4 with n3(q)=3 and n4(q)=4. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the Engel case, the growth conditions n3(q)=3 and n4(q)=4, the fact that the relevant spheres are 3-dimensional hypersurfaces in R^4, and that the singular behavior to classify occurs where an optimal singular curve meets such a sphere. Those are exactly the cues Agrachev uses when he passes from the Martinet question to the Engel one in Section IV. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))
missing_details: The paper asks for a C^1-classification of germs of spheres, not just a loose local classification of sphere singularities. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))

The scope is local near a base point q0, with q taken on a small sphere S_{q0}^{-1}(ε) centered at q0. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))

The metric assumption is generic: the question is posed for generic sub-Riemannian structures / generic metrics, and your draft does not state that. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))

To make the Engel hypothesis stand alone, n_k(q) should be defined as the span at q of all iterated Lie brackets of a local frame f0,f1 of the rank-2 distribution Δ of bracket length at most k. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))

Because the Engel sentence says that one should repeat the preceding question, the same equivalence notion is intended: classify sphere germs up to germs of C^1-diffeomorphisms of the ambient space, now R^4 rather than R^3. That ambient-equivalence clause is implicit in your draft but explicit in the immediately preceding Martinet formulation. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))

The relevant point q is not any point on the sphere: it is a point reached from q0 by an optimal singular segment, i.e. where the singular curve issuing from q0 meets S_{q0}^{-1}(ε). ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))
refined_question: Let Δ=span{f0,f1} be a smooth rank-2 Engel distribution in a neighborhood of q0∈R^4, meaning that n3(q)=3 and n4(q)=4, where n_k(q) is the span at q of all iterated Lie brackets of f0,f1 of length at most k. In this Engel case, each point lies on a unique singular curve and sufficiently small singular segments are optimal. Equip Δ with a generic sub-Riemannian metric, let S_{q0}(q) denote the sub-Riemannian distance from q0, and fix ε>0 small. If q∈S_{q0}^{-1}(ε) is a point where the optimal singular curve issuing from q0 meets the sphere, what is the C^1-classification, up to germs of C^1-diffeomorphisms of R^4, of the germ at q of the 3-dimensional hypersurface S_{q0}^{-1}(ε)? ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))
justification: The draft unmistakably targets Section IV rather than another part of the paper: it repeats the Engel growth vector n3(q)=3, n4(q)=4, the uniqueness of the singular curve through each point, the optimality of its small segments, and the fact that spheres are hypersurfaces in R^4. Agrachev’s official formulation is slightly sharper than the draft: he first formulates the Martinet problem as a C^1-classification of sphere germs at points of optimal singular curves for generic metrics, defines C^1-equivalence via ambient C^1-diffeomorphisms, and then says that for the Engel distribution one should repeat the same question. The next paragraph explains that solving the 4-dimensional Engel case is the key local step for understanding the general rank-2 case in dimension n≥4, while the later 2-dimensional almost-Riemannian problem is presented only as a modification containing the main difficulty, not as a proved equivalent reformulation. ([paperzz.com](https://paperzz.com/doc/7063141/some-open-problems---sissa-people-personal-home-pages))
